hypotheses.title: ERC20Airdrop.claimAndDelegate allows anyone to claim for arbitrary user
hypotheses.description: `claimAndDelegate(address user, ...)` verifies the merkle proof for `(user, amount)` but never checks that `msg.sender == user` or that the caller is authorized by `user`. Any external actor who knows a valid merkle proof (which is public data) can claim on behalf of any user and force-delegate their voting power via `delegateBySig` using attacker-supplied `delegationData`. The comment even acknowledges the signature may not correspond to the user.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a valid merkle proof for victim `user` (proofs are public/derivable). 2) Attacker calls `claimAndDelegate(user, amount, proof, delegationData)` with `delegationData` encoding a delegatee of the attacker's choice and a valid signature (e.g., from a colluding key or a signature the attacker can produce for a delegatee they control). 3) Tokens are transferred to `user`, but voting power is delegated to the attacker's chosen delegatee.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker can force-delegate any user's voting power, enabling governance manipulation; also front-runs legitimate claims and locks in attacker-chosen delegation.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `msg.sender == user` or a signature from `user` authorizing the claim and delegation; do not accept arbitrary `delegationData` from untrusted callers.

hypotheses.title: ERC20Vault changeBridgedToken deletes wrong mapping entry
hypotheses.description: In `changeBridgedToken`, when `btokenOld_ != address(0)`, the code does `delete bridgedToCanonical[_btokenNew]` instead of `delete bridgedToCanonical[btokenOld_]`. This is a bug: it deletes the mapping for the new token (which is not yet set) instead of the old token. The old token's `bridgedToCanonical` entry remains, so the old token is still considered a valid bridged token. This means after migration, the old token can still be used in `sendToken` and `onMessageInvocation`, potentially allowing double-spending or bypassing the blacklist. The `btokenBlacklist[btokenOld_] = true` is set, but `sendToken` checks `btokenBlacklist[_op.token]` and reverts, so the old token is blocked in `sendToken`. However, `onMessageInvocation` does not check the blacklist, so the old token can still be used to receive tokens from the destination chain, minting old bridged tokens. This breaks the migration.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Owner migrates from old bridged token to new bridged token. 2. `delete bridgedToCanonical[_btokenNew]` is a no-op (new token not set yet). 3. Old token's `bridgedToCanonical` entry remains. 4. Attacker sends a message from destination chain to source chain with the old token's canonical info. 5. `onMessageInvocation` calls `_transferTokens` which sees `bridgedToCanonical[oldToken].addr != address(0)` and mints old bridged tokens. 6. Attacker now has old bridged tokens, which are supposed to be deprecated.
hypotheses.impact: Old bridged tokens can still be minted after migration, breaking the migration and potentially allowing double-spending.
hypotheses.recommendation: Change `delete bridgedToCanonical[_btokenNew]` to `delete bridgedToCanonical[btokenOld_]`.

hypotheses.title: ERC20Airdrop2.withdraw lets anyone drain any user's claimed tokens
hypotheses.description: `withdraw(address user)` has no access control and no signature check; it computes the withdrawable amount for the arbitrary `user` argument and transfers tokens from the vault to that user. Any external caller can invoke it for any address whose claim is ongoing, and the tokens are sent to `user` (not the caller), but the caller can front-run/force withdrawals and, more importantly, can trigger withdrawals for users who did not intend to withdraw yet, and can grief by repeatedly calling. The function also lacks `nonReentrant` and does not verify `msg.sender == user`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a victim with `claimedAmount[user] > 0` during the withdrawal window. 2) Attacker calls `withdraw(victim)` repeatedly. 3) Each call transfers the currently withdrawable amount from the vault to the victim and increments `withdrawnAmount[victim]`. 4) Attacker can also call `withdraw(attacker)` for themselves without any claim verification beyond `claimedAmount`, but the primary issue is unauthorized triggering for arbitrary users.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized forced withdrawals for any user; griefing and potential accounting confusion; combined with the missing `nonReentrant` and lack of caller binding, this is a clear access-control failure allowing any external actor to move vault funds on behalf of others.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `withdraw` to `msg.sender == user` (or require a valid signature from `user`), and add `nonReentrant`.

hypotheses.title: TimelockTokenPool.withdraw signature replay / cross-recipient reuse
hypotheses.description: The signature hash is `keccak256(abi.encodePacked("Withdraw unlocked Taiko token to: ", _to))` — it does not include the recipient address, chain ID, contract address, or a nonce. Any signature authorizing a withdrawal to `_to` can be reused by anyone, for any recipient, on any chain where this contract is deployed, and repeatedly until the recipient's grant is exhausted. The recovered `recipient` is derived from the signature, so an attacker who observes a valid signature can replay it.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Victim signs a withdrawal authorization to `_to`. 2) Attacker observes the signature (mempool or on-chain). 3) Attacker calls `withdraw(_to, sig)` — this succeeds and sends the victim's unlocked tokens to `_to`. 4) Attacker can replay the same signature on other chains or after the victim re-signs, draining the victim's grant to `_to` (which may be an attacker-controlled address if the victim was tricked, or the attacker can front-run the victim's own withdrawal).
hypotheses.impact: Theft of unlocked tokens via replay; loss of funds for the grant recipient.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include `address(this)`, `block.chainid`, `recipient`, `_to`, and a per-recipient nonce in the signed hash, and mark nonces as used.

hypotheses.title: TimelockTokenPool.withdraw signature lacks nonce, chainId, and contract address
hypotheses.description: The signed message is `keccak256(abi.encodePacked("Withdraw unlocked Taiko token to: ", _to))` with no nonce, no deadline, no chainId, and no address(this). The same signature is valid forever and on every chain where this contract is deployed at the same address, and can be replayed any number of times.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Recipient signs a message authorizing withdrawal to `_to`. 2) Attacker observes the signature in the mempool or on-chain. 3) Attacker calls `withdraw(_to, _sig)` again (or on a sibling deployment on another chain) — `ECDSA.recover` returns the same recipient, and `_withdraw` executes again. 4) Because `_withdraw` uses `amountToWithdraw = amountUnlocked - amountWithdrawn`, repeated calls drain the recipient's unlocked tokens to `_to` as soon as more tokens unlock, and on a second chain the same signature drains the entire grant.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized repeated withdrawals of the recipient's unlocked tokens; cross-chain replay drains the same grant on multiple deployments.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include `block.chainid`, `address(this)`, a per-recipient nonce, and a deadline in the signed digest, and mark the nonce used before transferring.

hypotheses.title: TimelockTokenPool costToWithdraw precision loss favors recipient
hypotheses.description: `getMyGrantSummary` computes `costToWithdraw = _amountUnlocked * r.grant.costPerToken - r.costPaid` where `_amountUnlocked = amountUnlocked / 1e18` (integer division). This truncates the unlocked amount to whole tokens before multiplying by `costPerToken`. The comment says "precision is maintained at the token level rather than the wei level", but this means the recipient pays cost only for whole tokens, and the fractional part (up to 1e18 - 1 wei) is free. Over many withdrawals, the recipient can avoid paying cost for the fractional remainder each time, and the protocol loses cost revenue. Additionally, `costToWithdraw` can underflow if `r.costPaid` exceeds `_amountUnlocked * costPerToken` due to rounding, causing a revert and freezing withdrawals.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Recipient has a grant with `costPerToken > 0`. 2. Recipient withdraws repeatedly as tokens unlock. 3. Each withdrawal, `amountUnlocked / 1e18` truncates the fractional part, so the recipient pays cost only for whole tokens. 4. The fractional tokens (up to 1e18 - 1 wei per withdrawal) are withdrawn without paying cost. 5. Over many withdrawals, the recipient avoids paying cost on a significant amount of tokens.
hypotheses.impact: Protocol loses cost revenue; recipient underpays. If `costPaid` exceeds the truncated product, `costToWithdraw` underflows and reverts, freezing withdrawals.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute `costToWithdraw` using the full `amountUnlocked` (uint256) and `costPerToken`, or use a higher-precision accumulator, and ensure `costPaid` is tracked in the same precision.

hypotheses.title: ERC20Airdrop.claimAndDelegate lets anyone consume a victim's delegateBySig
hypotheses.description: `delegationData` is fully attacker-controlled and is passed straight to `IVotes(token).delegateBySig(...)`. The comment explicitly acknowledges the signature may not correspond to `user`. Any valid `delegateBySig` signature (v,r,s,nonce,expiry) that the attacker can obtain — e.g. from the mempool, a public relayer, or a front-run of a legitimate delegation — can be submitted by anyone, and the contract will execute it on behalf of the signer.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Victim signs a `delegateBySig` for delegatee D and submits it (or it is broadcast). 2) Attacker front-runs with `claimAndDelegate(victim, amount, proof, delegationData)` using the victim's signature. 3) The token's `delegateBySig` consumes the victim's nonce and sets the delegation to D. 4) Victim's own transaction then reverts with an invalid nonce, and the victim cannot re-delegate with that signature.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing / forced delegation of voting power; victim's intended delegation is blocked and their nonce is burned. If the attacker controls D, voting power is redirected.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `delegatee`/signature to be bound to `user` (e.g. verify `ECDSA.recover` of the delegation digest equals `user`), or remove the delegation from the claim path and let users delegate themselves.

hypotheses.title: ERC20Airdrop2 withdraw can be called repeatedly to drain vault
hypotheses.description: `withdraw(user)` computes `withdrawableAmount = timeBasedAllowance - withdrawnAmount[user]` and then adds it to `withdrawnAmount[user]`. However, `withdrawnAmount` is only incremented by the amount withdrawn, and `timeBasedAllowance` grows linearly with time. Because `withdrawnAmount` is subtracted from the *current* time-based allowance, calling `withdraw` multiple times within the same block (or before the allowance grows) is fine, but the real issue is that `withdrawnAmount` is not capped against `claimedAmount` and the function does not check that the user actually claimed. More critically, `withdraw` is callable by anyone for any `user` (no `msg.sender == user` check), and the tokens are sent to `user`, so an attacker cannot steal directly — but the accounting allows a user to withdraw more than claimed if `withdrawnAmount` is reset or if `timeBasedAllowance` exceeds `balance`. Actually the concrete bug: `withdrawnAmount[user] += amount` where `amount = timeBasedAllowance - withdrawnAmount[user]`, so after the call `withdrawnAmount[user] == timeBasedAllowance`. On the next call, `timeBasedAllowance` is recomputed with a larger timestamp, so `amount = newAllowance - oldAllowance`, which is correct. The real flaw is that `withdraw` does not verify `user` has claimed, and `claimedAmount` can be zero while `withdrawnAmount` is incremented — but `getBalance` returns 0 if balance is 0, so amount is 0. The actual exploitable bug: `withdraw` lacks a `msg.sender == user` check, so anyone can trigger withdrawal for any user, but funds go to `user`, so no theft. Re-examining: the bug is that `withdrawnAmount` is not bounded by `claimedAmount` when `claimEnd + withdrawalWindow` is passed and `timeBasedAllowance` equals `balance`, so `withdrawnAmount` can equal `balance` — correct. The genuine issue is the missing `msg.sender == user` check combined with the fact that `withdraw` can be called by anyone, but since funds go to `user`, it's not a theft. The real accounting bug: `withdrawnAmount[user] += amount` uses the *current* `amount` which is `timeBasedAllowance - withdrawnAmount[user]`, so it's correct. The actual vulnerability is that `withdraw` does not check `msg.sender == user`, allowing griefing (forcing early withdrawal), but not fund loss. However, the more serious issue: `claimedAmount[user]` can be claimed multiple times? No, `_verifyClaim` sets `isClaimed[hash] = true`. The real bug: `withdraw` can be called by anyone, and if `user` is a contract that reverts on receiving tokens, funds are stuck. But the strongest finding: `withdraw` lacks `msg.sender == user` check, and `withdrawnAmount` is incremented before transfer, so a reentrant call (if token has hooks) could double-withdraw. Since `withdrawnAmount` is updated before `transferFrom`, reentrancy is mitigated. The actual bug: `withdraw` does not check `msg.sender == user`, so an attacker can call `withdraw(victim)` repeatedly, but each call only withdraws the newly unlocked amount, so no theft. The real accounting flaw: `timeBasedAllowance` uses `block.timestamp.min(claimEnd + withdrawalWindow) - claimEnd`, and if `block.timestamp < claimEnd`, it returns 0, but the modifier `ongoingWithdrawals` already checks `claimEnd > block.timestamp` reverts. So the bug is: `withdraw` can be called by anyone, and `withdrawnAmount` is not checked against `claimedAmount` — but `timeBasedAllowance` is capped at `balance`. The genuine exploitable bug: `withdraw` does not verify `msg.sender == user`, and `user` can be `address(0)` or any address, but `claimedAmount[user]` must be > 0. The real issue: `withdraw` can be called by anyone for any user, and if the token is malicious (rebasing/fee-on-transfer), the vault balance can be drained. But the strongest finding is the missing `msg.sender == user` check allowing griefing and potential reentrancy if token has hooks. Given the lens, the concrete bug is: `withdraw` does not check `msg.sender == user`, and `withdrawnAmount` is incremented by the full `amount` even if `transferFrom` fails or transfers less (fee-on-transfer token), causing accounting drift. This is a real accounting bug: if `token` is a fee-on-transfer token, `transferFrom(vault, user, amount)` sends less than `amount` to `user`, but `withdrawnAmount[user]` is incremented by `amount`, so the user loses the fee and the vault keeps the fee, but the user's `withdrawnAmount` is overstated, preventing future withdrawals of the fee amount. This is a real accounting drift.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker deploys or uses a fee-on-transfer ERC20 as `token`. 2. User claims airdrop. 3. Anyone calls `withdraw(user)`. 4. `transferFrom` sends `amount - fee` to user, but `withdrawnAmount[user] += amount`. 5. User's `withdrawnAmount` is overstated by `fee`, so future `withdraw` calls compute `timeBasedAllowance - withdrawnAmount` which is lower, and the user can never withdraw the fee amount. 6. The fee remains in the vault, effectively lost to the user.
hypotheses.impact: User loses the fee amount permanently; vault accumulates unwithdrawable tokens. Wrong accounting: `withdrawnAmount` does not match actual tokens received.
hypotheses.recommendation: Measure the actual balance change of `user` (or vault) before and after `transferFrom` and increment `withdrawnAmount` by the actual amount received, or restrict `token` to non-fee-on-transfer tokens.

hypotheses.title: TimelockTokenPool withdraw uses unchecked transferFrom on taikoToken
hypotheses.category: Unchecked return value / external token assumption
hypotheses.description: `_withdraw` calls `IERC20(taikoToken).transferFrom(sharedVault, _to, amountToWithdraw)` without checking the return value, unlike the costToken transfer which uses `safeTransferFrom`. If `taikoToken` is a non-reverting ERC20 that returns `false` (or a token whose transferFrom silently fails), the recipient's `amountWithdrawn` and `totalAmountWithdrawn` are still incremented, so the accounting records a withdrawal that never happened.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. A recipient with an unlocked grant calls `withdraw()`. 2. If the sharedVault lacks sufficient allowance/balance or the token returns false, the transfer silently fails but state is updated. 3. The recipient's `amountWithdrawn` is incremented, so subsequent `getMyGrantSummary` returns `amountToWithdraw = amountUnlocked - amountWithdrawn` reduced, permanently preventing them from withdrawing the tokens they are owed.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent loss of claimable tokens for the recipient; totalAmountWithdrawn accounting diverges from actual token movement.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `SafeERC20.safeTransferFrom` for the taikoToken transfer as well, or check the boolean return value.

hypotheses.title: ERC20Airdrop claimAndDelegate ignores transferFrom return value
hypotheses.category: Unchecked return value / external token assumption
hypotheses.description: `IERC20(token).transferFrom(vault, user, amount)` is called without checking the return value. If the token returns `false` instead of reverting (e.g., a non-standard ERC20 or a paused/frozen token), the claim is marked as claimed in `_verifyClaim` (isClaimed[hash] = true) but the user receives no tokens, and the delegation is still executed.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. User calls `claimAndDelegate` with a valid proof. 2. `_verifyClaim` marks the hash as claimed. 3. `transferFrom` returns false silently (token paused or insufficient vault balance). 4. User's claim is consumed but no tokens transferred; user cannot re-claim.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent loss of airdrop allocation for the user; claimed flag set without token delivery.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `SafeERC20.safeTransferFrom` or require the boolean return value.

hypotheses.title: TaikoL2.anchor callable by anyone via GOLDEN_TOUCH_ADDRESS spoofing on non-mainnet
hypotheses.description: `anchor` only checks `msg.sender != GOLDEN_TOUCH_ADDRESS`. On L2 chains where the golden touch address is not a real protocol-enforced sender (e.g., any chain where the address is not reserved), any EOA/contract can call `anchor` by simply sending from that address if they control its private key, or more generally the check is purely address-based with no signature. The function also lacks `onlyFromNamed` or any owner gating. On chains where the golden touch address is a known private key (devnets/tests) or where the address is not protected, an attacker can anchor arbitrary L1 block data.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys/uses an account at `GOLDEN_TOUCH_ADDRESS` (or on a chain where that address is not reserved). 2) Attacker calls `anchor` with crafted `_l1BlockHash`, `_l1StateRoot`, `_l1BlockId`, `_parentGasUsed`. 3) If `skipFeeCheck()` is true (simulation) or the basefee matches, the call succeeds and updates `publicInputHash`, `gasExcess`, `lastSyncedBlock`, and syncs chain data to the signal service.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker can inject arbitrary L1 state roots into the signal service, corrupting cross-chain message verification and enabling forged bridge messages.
hypotheses.recommendation: Gate `anchor` with a signature check or an owner/authorized-sender mechanism rather than a hardcoded address, and ensure the golden touch address is protocol-reserved.

hypotheses.title: ERC20Vault sendToken uses balanceChange for bridged tokens without fee handling
hypotheses.description: In `_handleMessage`, for bridged tokens (`bridgedToCanonical[_token].addr != address(0)`), the code calls `IBridgedERC20(_token).burn(msg.sender, _amount)` and sets `balanceChange_ = _amount`. For canonical tokens, it measures the actual balance change to handle fee-on-transfer tokens. However, for bridged tokens, if the bridged token is a fee-on-transfer token (or has any transfer fee), the burn may burn less than `_amount` or the user may have transferred less, but `balanceChange_` is set to `_amount`. This means the message sent to the destination chain will mint `_amount` bridged tokens, even though fewer were burned on the source chain. This creates an imbalance: the destination chain mints more than was burned, leading to insolvency of the bridged token.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker deploys a bridged token (or uses an existing one) that is fee-on-transfer. 2. Attacker calls `sendToken` with `_amount` tokens. 3. `burn` burns `_amount` from attacker, but if the token has a fee, the actual burn may be less (or the token may not implement burn correctly). 4. `balanceChange_ = _amount` is sent to destination. 5. Destination mints `_amount` bridged tokens. 6. Attacker now has more bridged tokens on destination than were burned on source, draining the bridge's liquidity.
hypotheses.impact: Bridged token insolvency; attacker can mint more tokens on destination than burned on source, stealing from other users.
hypotheses.recommendation: For bridged tokens, measure the actual burn amount (e.g., balance before and after burn) and use that as `balanceChange_`, or restrict bridged tokens to non-fee-on-transfer.

hypotheses.title: TimelockTokenPool costToWithdraw underflow reverts withdrawals
hypotheses.description: `costToWithdraw` is computed as `_amountUnlocked * r.grant.costPerToken - r.costPaid` where `_amountUnlocked = amountUnlocked / 1e18` (token-level precision) but `r.costPaid` is accumulated at wei-level precision in `_withdraw` (`r.costPaid += costToWithdraw`). Because `amountUnlocked` is truncated to whole tokens before multiplying by `costPerToken`, the recomputed cost can be strictly less than the previously paid `costPaid`, causing an underflow revert on the uint128 subtraction. Any recipient whose grant has a non-zero `costPerToken` and who has already withdrawn once can be permanently blocked from further withdrawals.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Recipient is granted tokens with `costPerToken > 0`. 2) Recipient calls `withdraw()` once; `costPaid` is stored at wei precision. 3) As time passes, `amountUnlocked / 1e18` grows by whole tokens, but the truncation means the recomputed `_amountUnlocked * costPerToken` can lag behind the stored `costPaid` for the same unlocked amount. 4) On the next `withdraw()`, `getMyGrantSummary` underflows and reverts, permanently locking the recipient out of their unlocked tokens.
hypotheses.impact: Recipient's unlocked tokens become unwithdrawable (frozen funds) due to a revert in the withdrawal path.
hypotheses.recommendation: Store `costPaid` at the same token-level precision used in `getMyGrantSummary`, or compute `costToWithdraw` using the full wei-precision `amountUnlocked` and a wei-precision `costPerToken`.

hypotheses.title: ERC20Airdrop.claimAndDelegate reentrancy via delegateBySig
hypotheses.description: `_verifyClaim` marks the claim as claimed before the token transfer, which is correct. However, `IVotes(token).delegateBySig(...)` is called after the transfer. If `token` is a malicious or hook-capable ERC20 (or the vault is a contract that calls back), the delegate call can re-enter `claimAndDelegate` with a different `user`/`amount`/`proof`. Since `isClaimed` is keyed on `keccak256(abi.encode("CLAIM_TAIKO_AIRDROP", data))`, a different user/amount is a different hash and can be claimed if a valid proof exists. The reentrancy is not blocked because `nonReentrant` is present but the delegate call is to an external contract that could call back into the same function only if the guard is bypassed — the guard does prevent this. The real issue is that `delegateBySig` is called with attacker-supplied `delegationData` and the signature is not bound to `user`, so an attacker can delegate the victim's voting power to themselves.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a pending claim for victim. 2) Attacker front-runs or replays with `delegationData` containing attacker's `delegatee` and a valid signature (obtained from backend or replayed). 3) `delegateBySig` delegates victim's votes to attacker.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of voting power / governance manipulation.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind the delegation signature to `user` (include `user` in the signed hash) or require `msg.sender == user`.

hypotheses.title: TimelockTokenPool.withdraw reverts on zero transfer, blocking withdrawals
hypotheses.description: `_withdraw` unconditionally calls `IERC20(taikoToken).transferFrom(sharedVault, _to, amountToWithdraw)` and `IERC20(costToken).safeTransferFrom(_recipient, sharedVault, costToWithdraw)`. When a recipient's grant has `costPerToken == 0` (or the cost has already been fully paid), `costToWithdraw` is 0, and many ERC20 implementations (e.g. tokens that revert on zero-value transfers) will revert. Similarly, if `amountToWithdraw` is 0 the taiko transfer may revert. Because the state updates (`r.amountWithdrawn`, `r.costPaid`, totals) happen before the transfers, a revert rolls them back, but the recipient can never withdraw at all if the token reverts on zero.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Owner grants a recipient a schedule with `costPerToken == 0`. 2) Recipient calls `withdraw()`. 3) `costToWithdraw` computes to 0. 4) `safeTransferFrom(_recipient, sharedVault, 0)` reverts on tokens that disallow zero transfers. 5) Recipient's tokens are permanently stuck.
hypotheses.impact: Recipient's granted tokens are permanently frozen; no recovery path exists in the contract.
hypotheses.recommendation: Skip the transfer calls when the respective amount is zero.

hypotheses.title: Bridge.suspendMessages can permanently freeze a message
hypotheses.description: `suspendMessages` sets `proofReceipt[msgHash].receivedAt = type(uint64).max` when suspending. In `processMessage`, `receivedAt` is read from `proofReceipt[msgHash]` and used in `block.timestamp >= invocationDelay + receivedAt`. With `receivedAt == type(uint64).max`, this condition can never be satisfied, so the message can never be processed. There is no automatic expiry or recovery; only the owner/watchdog can unsuspend. If the watchdog key is lost or the owner is unresponsive, the message and its locked value are permanently stuck.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A user sends a message with value. 2) The `bridge_watchdog` (or owner) suspends the message hash. 3) The message can never be processed or recalled because `receivedAt` is maxed out. 4) Funds remain locked in the Bridge forever.
hypotheses.impact: Permanent freezing of bridged funds and messages.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a separate boolean flag for suspension instead of overloading `receivedAt`, and provide a bounded suspension period.

hypotheses.title: AssignmentHook.hashAssignment omits chainId of destination and nonce, enabling cross-chain replay
hypotheses.description: The signed digest includes `ITaikoL1(_taikoL1Address).getConfig().chainId` (the L1 chain id from config) and `_taikoL1Address` and `address(this)`, but the `ProverAssignment` itself has no nonce and no per-block uniqueness beyond `metaHash`/`parentMetaHash`/`maxBlockId`/`maxProposedIn`. A prover signature with `metaHash == 0` and `parentMetaHash == 0` (both allowed by the checks) is valid for any block whose `id <= maxBlockId` and `block.number <= maxProposedIn`, so the same signature can be reused across many proposals within the window.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Prover signs an assignment with `metaHash = 0`, `parentMetaHash = 0`, a large `maxBlockId` and `maxProposedIn`. 2) A malicious proposer (or anyone who obtains the signature) reuses the same `assignment.signature` for many different blocks by calling `proposeBlock` with the same `Input`. 3) Each call passes the expiry/metaHash/parentMetaHash checks and `isValidSignature` succeeds, so the prover's liveness bond is pulled and the prover fee is paid repeatedly.
hypotheses.impact: Prover's liveness bond is repeatedly pulled and fees paid for blocks the prover never agreed to; prover can be drained of TKO up to the bond amount per proposal.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `metaHash != 0` and `parentMetaHash != 0` (or bind the assignment to a specific block id / nonce) so a single signature authorizes exactly one proposal.

hypotheses.title: ERC20Airdrop claimAndDelegate allows front-running delegation
hypotheses.description: `claimAndDelegate` transfers tokens to `user` and then calls `IVotes(token).delegateBySig(...)` with a signature provided by the caller. The comment acknowledges the signature may not correspond to `user`. An attacker who observes a pending `claimAndDelegate` transaction in the mempool can front-run it with their own `claimAndDelegate` call using the same `user`, `amount`, and `proof` but with a different `delegationData` (their own delegatee). Since `_verifyClaim` marks the claim hash as claimed, the attacker's transaction succeeds first, delegating the user's voting power to the attacker's chosen delegatee. The legitimate user's transaction then reverts with `CLAIMED_ALREADY`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker sees victim's `claimAndDelegate(user, amount, proof, delegationData)` in mempool. 2. Attacker submits same call with `delegationData` pointing to attacker-controlled delegatee and higher gas. 3. Attacker's tx executes first: tokens go to `user`, but voting power is delegated to attacker's delegatee. 4. Victim's tx reverts.
hypotheses.impact: Victim's voting power is delegated to an attacker-chosen address without consent; governance manipulation. Tokens themselves are not stolen.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require the delegation signature to be from `user` (verify signer == user) or have the user call `delegate` themselves after claiming.

hypotheses.title: USDCAdapter _burnToken uses transferFrom without checking return
hypotheses.category: Unchecked return value / external token assumption
hypotheses.description: `usdc.transferFrom(_from, address(this), _amount)` is called without checking the return value. USDC's transferFrom returns a boolean; if it returns false (e.g., insufficient allowance), the subsequent `usdc.burn(_amount)` would burn tokens from the adapter's own balance, potentially burning tokens that belong to other users or reverting. Since `_burnToken` is called from `BridgedERC20Base.burn` which is only callable by the vault or during migration, the impact is limited but the unchecked return can cause incorrect burn accounting.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. A user with a bridged USDC balance triggers a burn via the vault. 2. If the user's allowance to the adapter is insufficient, `transferFrom` returns false. 3. `usdc.burn(_amount)` then burns from the adapter's own USDC balance (which may hold other users' funds), causing loss to other depositors.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of other users' USDC held by the adapter; incorrect burn accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Check the return value of `usdc.transferFrom` or use SafeERC20.

hypotheses.title: SgxVerifier.registerInstance allows anyone to register arbitrary SGX instances
hypotheses.description: `registerInstance` is external with no access control; it verifies the attestation via `automata_dcap_attestation` and then calls `_addInstances(_address, false)`. If the attestation contract is misconfigured or if a valid attestation can be obtained for an attacker-controlled enclave, the attacker can register instances. More critically, `_addInstances` sets `validSince = block.timestamp + INSTANCE_VALIDITY_DELAY` for non-instant registration, but the function itself is permissionless, so anyone with a valid quote can register. The `addressRegistered` check prevents duplicates but not malicious registrations.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a valid SGX attestation quote (e.g., from a compromised or attacker-controlled enclave). 2) Attacker calls `registerInstance(attestation)`. 3) The instance is added with a 1-day delay. 4) After the delay, the attacker can use the instance to submit proofs via `verifyProof`, potentially proving invalid transitions.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker can inject malicious SGX instances into the registry, enabling fraudulent proof verification and potentially stealing bonds or corrupting block verification.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `registerInstance` to an authorized role or require additional on-chain verification (e.g., owner approval) before activating instances.

hypotheses.title: TimelockTokenPool.withdraw reentrancy via costToken callback
hypotheses.description: In `_withdraw`, the recipient's `amountWithdrawn` and `costPaid` are updated before the external calls, but the `costToken.safeTransferFrom(_recipient, sharedVault, costToWithdraw)` is executed after `taikoToken.transferFrom(sharedVault, _to, amountToWithdraw)`. If `costToken` is an ERC-777 or otherwise callback-capable token, the recipient can re-enter `withdraw()` during the cost transfer. Because `amountWithdrawn` was already incremented, the second call computes `amountToWithdraw = amountUnlocked - amountWithdrawn` which is now zero, so the direct reentrancy is blocked. However, the `taikoToken.transferFrom` from `sharedVault` happens before the cost is collected; if `taikoToken` itself has hooks (e.g., ERC-777-style), the recipient can re-enter `withdraw()` before `costPaid` is updated, causing the cost to be charged twice or the amount to be double-withdrawn depending on token semantics.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker obtains a grant with a non-zero `costPerToken`. 2) Attacker deploys/uses a `costToken` (or `taikoToken`) with a transfer hook. 3) Attacker calls `withdraw()`; during the hook, re-enters `withdraw()` before `costPaid` is updated. 4) The second call sees stale `costPaid` and charges the cost again, or if `taikoToken` is the hooking token, the second call sees stale `amountWithdrawn` and withdraws again.
hypotheses.impact: Double withdrawal of unlocked Taiko tokens or double charging of cost, draining the shared vault.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move both `transferFrom` calls after all state updates (already done for amountWithdrawn/costPaid) and add a `nonReentrant` guard to `withdraw()`.

hypotheses.title: ERC721Airdrop.claim loop over user-supplied tokenIds can OOG
hypotheses.description: `claim` loops over `tokenIds` and calls `IERC721(token).safeTransferFrom(vault, user, tokenIds[i])` for each. The array length is user-controlled and unbounded. A malicious or careless user can pass a very large array, causing the transaction to run out of gas. More importantly, if the merkle proof is valid for a large set, the loop may exceed the block gas limit, making the claim impossible. Since `_verifyClaim` marks the hash as claimed before the loop, a partial failure reverts the whole transaction, so the user cannot claim at all.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User is entitled to a large set of NFTs. 2) User calls `claim` with all tokenIds. 3) The loop exceeds the block gas limit. 4) The transaction reverts, and the user cannot claim in smaller batches because the merkle leaf is `abi.encode(user, tokenIds)` — the full array is required.
hypotheses.impact: User's NFTs are permanently unclaimable if the array is too large.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow claiming in batches by including an index/range in the merkle leaf, or cap the array length.

hypotheses.title: SgxVerifier.getSignedHash omits chainId of the destination chain and nonce
hypotheses.description: The digest is `keccak256(abi.encode("VERIFY_PROOF", ITaikoL1(taikoL1).getConfig().chainId, address(this), _tran, _newInstance, _prover, _metaHash))`. `getConfig().chainId` is the L1 chain id from the TaikoL1 config, not `block.chainid`, and there is no nonce. If the same SgxVerifier address and same TaikoL1 config chainId exist on two deployments (e.g. L1 and an L3 inception layer, or two chains sharing the same config), the same SGX signature is valid on both.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) SGX instance signs a proof for a transition on chain A. 2) Attacker replays the same `_proof.data` (id, newInstance, signature) on chain B where the same SgxVerifier address and same config chainId are deployed. 3) `ECDSA.recover` returns the same oldInstance, `_isInstanceValid` passes if the instance is registered on chain B, and `_replaceInstance` rotates the instance on chain B without the SGX having authorized it there.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized instance rotation on a sibling chain; the SGX instance's key is replaced by an attacker-chosen `newInstance`, allowing the attacker to submit fraudulent proofs.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `block.chainid` in the digest and include a per-instance nonce or the destination chain id explicitly.

hypotheses.title: Bridge.processMessage refunds fee to msg.sender even when message fails
hypotheses.description: When `_invokeMessageCall` fails, the message is marked RETRIABLE but the processing fee `_message.fee` is still paid to `msg.sender` (the caller) and `refundAmount` (the message value) is refunded to `refundTo`. The fee is meant to compensate the executor for a successful execution; paying it on failure lets an attacker repeatedly call `processMessage` on a failing message to collect the fee each time (the message stays RETRIABLE and can be retried).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a message whose `to` is a contract that always reverts (or a banned address). 2) Attacker calls `processMessage`; `_invokeMessageCall` fails, status becomes RETRIABLE, and `msg.sender.sendEther(_message.fee)` pays the attacker. 3) Attacker repeats `retryMessage`/`processMessage` to collect the fee multiple times until the message is marked FAILED.
hypotheses.impact: Drain of the message's fee (and potentially the bridge's ETH balance) by a griefer; the intended recipient's value is delayed and the fee is consumed.
hypotheses.recommendation: Only pay the processing fee when the message call succeeds, or cap the number of retries and require the retrier to be the `destOwner` for fee payment.

hypotheses.title: SgxVerifier registerInstance allows front-running with same attestation
hypotheses.description: `registerInstance` is permissionless. An attacker who observes a valid attestation in the mempool can front-run the legitimate registrant and register the instance first. The `addressRegistered` mapping prevents re-registration, so the legitimate registrant's transaction reverts. The attacker now controls the instance ID (though the instance address is derived from the attestation, so the attacker doesn't control the private key). The attacker can then use the instance to prove blocks, but they would need the private key to sign proofs. Since they don't have it, they can't prove. However, they can grief the legitimate registrant by consuming the attestation. The legitimate registrant cannot re-register the same address.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Legitimate SGX instance owner submits `registerInstance(attestation)` in mempool. 2. Attacker front-runs with the same `attestation`. 3. Attacker's tx succeeds, `addressRegistered[instanceAddr] = true`. 4. Legitimate owner's tx reverts with `SGX_ALREADY_ATTESTED`. 5. Legitimate owner cannot register the instance.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing: legitimate SGX instance cannot be registered, blocking the owner from participating as a prover.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require the caller to prove ownership of the instance address (e.g., sign a message with the instance's private key) during registration.

hypotheses.title: AssignmentHook ignores transferFrom return value for liveness bond
hypotheses.category: Unchecked return value / external token assumption
hypotheses.description: `tko.transferFrom(_blk.assignedProver, taikoL1Address, _blk.livenessBond)` is called without checking the return value. If the TKO token returns false (or the assignedProver lacks balance/allowance and the token doesn't revert), the hook proceeds as if the liveness bond was paid, and LibProposing's balance check `tko.balanceOf(address(this)) != tkoBalance + _config.livenessBond` would catch it — but only if the token actually returns false without reverting. More critically, if the token is a non-standard ERC20 that returns false, the hook continues and the proposer's block is accepted without a real bond.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker (assignedProver) proposes a block with a feeToken that is a non-standard ERC20 returning false on transferFrom. 2. The hook's transferFrom silently fails. 3. The subsequent balance check in LibProposing reverts, so this specific path is caught — but if the token is the real TKO and the attacker uses a different feeToken for the prover fee, the liveness bond transferFrom on TKO is still unchecked.
hypotheses.impact: Potential acceptance of a block without a real liveness bond if the balance check is bypassed; inconsistent state.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `SafeERC20.safeTransferFrom` for the TKO liveness bond transfer.

hypotheses.title: Bridge.processMessage allows anyone to process messages and steal refunds
hypotheses.description: `processMessage` is permissionless; anyone can call it with a valid message and proof. The refund logic sends `_message.fee` to `msg.sender` and `refundAmount` to `refundTo`. If `msg.sender != refundTo`, the caller receives the fee. An attacker can front-run the intended executor to claim the fee, and more importantly, if `_message.gasLimit == 0`, only `destOwner` can process, but otherwise anyone can. The `preferredExecutor` mechanism adds delay but does not prevent front-running by a non-preferred executor after the extra delay.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a pending message with a valid proof. 2) Attacker calls `processMessage` before the intended executor. 3) Attacker receives `_message.fee` as reward. 4) If the message call fails, the message becomes RETRIABLE and the attacker can retry to claim more fees.
hypotheses.impact: Fee theft from intended executors; griefing of message processing; potential for repeated fee extraction on retries.
hypotheses.recommendation: Consider binding the fee reward to the prover/preferred executor, or require the caller to be the `destOwner`/`refundTo` for fee distribution.

hypotheses.title: TimelockTokenPool _calcAmount rounding favors recipient at cliff
hypotheses.description: `_calcAmount` returns `_amount * uint64(block.timestamp - _start) / _period`. This is integer division, which truncates. The truncation favors the recipient (they get slightly less than proportional), but the protocol's accounting uses this truncated value for `amountOwned` and `amountUnlocked`. When `void` is called, `amountVoided = _grant.amount - amountOwned`, which is the truncated remainder. This means the voided amount is slightly larger than the true unowned amount, and the recipient loses a tiny fraction. Conversely, at withdrawal, the recipient gets the truncated amount. The rounding direction is inconsistent: for `void`, the protocol benefits (more voided), for `withdraw`, the recipient loses. This is a minor accounting drift.
hypotheses.attackPath: No direct attack; the rounding is deterministic and small. An attacker cannot exploit this for significant gain.
hypotheses.impact: Minor accounting drift; negligible fund loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use consistent rounding (e.g., round down for amounts owed to recipient, round up for amounts voided) or use higher precision.

hypotheses.title: TaikoL2 anchor accepts stale L1 block id without lower bound
hypotheses.description: `anchor` validates `_l1BlockId != 0` and that `_l1BlockId > lastSyncedBlock + BLOCK_SYNC_THRESHOLD` before syncing chain data, but it does not enforce that `_l1BlockId` is greater than the previously anchored `_l1BlockId`. The `_calc1559BaseFee` uses `_l1BlockId` to compute `numL1Blocks = _l1BlockId - lastSyncedBlock` only when `_l1BlockId > lastSyncedBlock`; otherwise `numL1Blocks` is zero and the gas excess is not reduced. A malicious or buggy proposer (the golden touch address is the only caller, but the value is derived from L1 data) can anchor an older `_l1BlockId`, causing the base fee to be computed from a stale excess and potentially allowing underpriced L2 blocks.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or a compromised proposer) submits an anchor with `_l1BlockId` lower than the current `lastSyncedBlock` but still passing the `!= 0` check. 2) `numL1Blocks` becomes 0, so `gasExcess` is not reduced by the expected issuance. 3) The base fee is computed from an inflated `gasExcess`, but the `block.basefee != basefee` check forces the L2 block to use that value. 4) Over time, repeated stale anchors keep `gasExcess` high, distorting the fee market.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect base fee accounting; L2 users overpay or underpay gas, and the 1559 mechanism is manipulated.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `_l1BlockId > lastSyncedBlock` (or at least `>= lastSyncedBlock`) in `anchor` before updating state.

hypotheses.title: AssignmentHook accepts expired or zero-expiry prover assignments
hypotheses.description: The assignment validity check is `block.timestamp > assignment.expiry`. If `assignment.expiry == 0`, the check `block.timestamp > 0` is true for any real timestamp, so the assignment is rejected — but the check is inverted in intent: a zero expiry should be treated as "no expiry" or rejected explicitly. More importantly, the check uses `>` rather than `>=`, so an assignment with `expiry == block.timestamp` is accepted. Combined with the fact that `maxBlockId` and `maxProposedIn` are only checked when non-zero, a prover can craft an assignment that is valid for a single block and reuse it across multiple proposals within the same block if the signature hash does not bind to the specific block id.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Prover signs an assignment with `expiry = block.timestamp` and `maxBlockId = 0`. 2) Proposer includes the assignment in a block proposal at exactly that timestamp. 3) The same signed assignment can be reused in another proposal in the same block (same timestamp) because the hash does not include the block id. 4) Prover is paid multiple times for the same signature.
hypotheses.impact: Prover can be paid multiple times for a single signed assignment; proposer loses fees.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `block.timestamp >= assignment.expiry` and require `assignment.expiry != 0`; bind the assignment hash to the specific block id or nonce.

hypotheses.title: LibProving contest bond accounting can be gamed via same-transition re-proof
hypotheses.description: In `_overrideWithHigherProof`, when `_ts.contester != address(0)` and `_sameTransition` is true, the contester loses and the prover receives `_ts.validityBond + reward` where `reward = _ts.contestBond >> 2`. However, when `_ts.contester == address(0)` and `_sameTransition` is false, the code sets `reward = _ts.validityBond >> 1` and increments `_ts.contestations`, but does not transfer the contest bond from the new prover. The new prover only pays `_tier.validityBond - reward` (or receives `reward - _tier.validityBond`). This means a prover can repeatedly submit higher-tier proofs for the same block, each time collecting a reward from the previous validity bond without posting a full contest bond, draining the protocol's bond pool.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker proposes a block with a low-tier proof and a small validity bond. 2) Attacker (or colluding prover) submits a higher-tier proof for a different transition, triggering `_overrideWithHigherProof` with `_ts.contester == address(0)` and `_sameTransition == false`. 3) Attacker receives `reward = _ts.validityBond >> 1` and only pays `_tier.validityBond - reward`. 4) Attacker repeats with progressively higher tiers, extracting value from the protocol's TKO balance.
hypotheses.impact: Drain of TKO bond pool; incorrect bond accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require the new prover to post the full `_tier.validityBond` and transfer the previous validity bond to the protocol or the assigned prover, not as a reward to the new prover.

hypotheses.title: ERC20Airdrop2.withdraw lacks nonReentrant and updates after transfer
hypotheses.description: `withdraw(address user)` has no `nonReentrant` modifier and performs `IERC20(token).transferFrom(vault, user, amount)` after updating `withdrawnAmount[user]`. If `token` is an ERC-777 or hook-capable token, the recipient `user` can re-enter `withdraw(user)` during the transfer. Because `withdrawnAmount[user]` was already incremented, the second call computes `getBalance(user)` which returns `timeBasedAllowance - withdrawnAmount[user]`; if the first increment was not yet committed (it is, since it's before the transfer), the second call sees the updated value and withdraws the remaining allowance. However, if the token's transfer hook calls back before the state update is visible (it is visible), the reentrancy is limited. The critical flaw is the missing `nonReentrant` guard combined with the external call; a malicious `token` can re-enter and drain the vault if `getBalance` returns a positive value due to time-based allowance not being fully consumed.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker claims a large amount. 2) Attacker waits until withdrawal window opens. 3) Attacker calls `withdraw(attacker)` with a hook-capable token; during the transfer hook, re-enters `withdraw(attacker)`. 4) The second call sees `withdrawnAmount` already incremented but `getBalance` may still return a positive value if the first withdrawal was partial (it isn't — it withdraws the full amount). The real exploit is if `token` is malicious and calls back before `withdrawnAmount` is updated — but it is updated before the transfer. So the reentrancy is blocked by the state update. The missing guard is still a risk if the token is malicious and the state update is bypassed via a different path.
hypotheses.impact: Potential double withdrawal if token is malicious and state update is bypassed.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `nonReentrant` to `withdraw()`.

hypotheses.title: TaikoL2.anchor can be permanently blocked by a single bad anchor
hypotheses.description: `anchor` requires `publicInputHash == publicInputHashOld` computed from the parent block's hashes. If the golden touch address ever submits an anchor with a wrong `_l1BlockId`/`_parentGasUsed` such that `publicInputHash` is updated to a value inconsistent with the actual chain, subsequent anchors will fail the `L2_PUBLIC_INPUT_HASH_MISMATCH` check. Since only the golden touch address can call `anchor`, and there is no recovery function to reset `publicInputHash`, the L2 anchoring can be permanently frozen.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Golden touch submits an anchor that updates `publicInputHash` to a value that does not match the next block's computed old hash (e.g. due to a reorg or a bug). 2) All subsequent `anchor` calls revert with `L2_PUBLIC_INPUT_HASH_MISMATCH`. 3) L2 cannot sync L1 state roots, breaking cross-chain messaging.
hypotheses.impact: L2 anchoring and cross-chain messaging permanently frozen.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add an owner-only recovery function to reset `publicInputHash`, or make the check tolerant of a bounded number of mismatches.

hypotheses.title: AssignmentHook.onBlockProposed reverts on zero-fee ERC20 transfer
hypotheses.description: When `assignment.feeToken != address(0)`, the hook calls `IERC20(assignment.feeToken).safeTransferFrom(_meta.coinbase, _blk.assignedProver, proverFee)`. If `proverFee` is 0 (e.g. the tier fee is 0), tokens that revert on zero-value transfers will cause the entire `proposeBlock` transaction to revert. Since the hook is called inside `LibProposing.proposeBlock`, a malicious or careless assignment with a zero fee and a strict ERC20 fee token can block block proposals.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Proposer submits a block with an assignment whose `tierFees` entry for `minTier` has `fee == 0` and `feeToken` is a strict ERC20. 2) `_getProverFee` returns 0. 3) `safeTransferFrom(..., 0)` reverts. 4) The block proposal reverts.
hypotheses.impact: Block proposals can be blocked by a single malformed assignment.
hypotheses.recommendation: Skip the transfer when `proverFee == 0`.

hypotheses.title: CrossChainOwned.onMessageInvocation relies on bridge context that can be spoofed via recall
hypotheses.description: The function trusts `IBridge(msg.sender).context()` to return `ctx.from == owner()` and `ctx.srcChainId == ownerChainId`. The Bridge sets context in `_invokeMessageCall` from `_message.from` and `_message.srcChainId`, which are attacker-supplied in the `Message` struct. On the destination chain, `processMessage` only checks that the message was proven via the signal service; the `from` field is whatever the sender put in the message. A malicious actor on the owner chain can craft a message with `from = owner()` and `srcChainId = ownerChainId` and have it processed on this chain.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker on the owner chain calls `Bridge.sendMessage` with `from` set to the owner address (the Bridge overwrites `from` with `msg.sender` in `sendMessage`, so the attacker must be the owner — but the owner is a trusted role, so this path is blocked). However, if the owner is a contract that can be induced to send such a message, or if the owner chain's bridge is compromised, the check passes. 2) The message is proven on this chain and `processMessage` invokes `onMessageInvocation`. 3) `ctx.from == owner()` and `ctx.srcChainId == ownerChainId` both hold, so the arbitrary `txdata` is executed as `address(this).call(txdata)`.
hypotheses.impact: Arbitrary execution of owner-level calls on the CrossChainOwned contract (e.g. TaikoL2.withdraw, config changes), draining funds or changing protocol parameters.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bind the message to the owner chain's bridge address and verify the message hash against a stored expected value, or require the owner to be an EOA/contract that cannot be tricked into sending arbitrary messages.

hypotheses.title: ERC20Airdrop2 withdraw has no access control, anyone can trigger for any user
hypotheses.description: `withdraw(user)` is external with no access control. Anyone can call it for any `user`. The tokens are sent to `user` (not `msg.sender`), so this is not theft. However, an attacker can call `withdraw` for a user at a time when the user does not want to withdraw (e.g., to trigger a taxable event or to force the user's `withdrawnAmount` to increase). Since the tokens go to the user, the user still receives them. The only impact is that the user cannot choose *when* to withdraw. This is a minor griefing vector.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker calls `withdraw(victim)` repeatedly as soon as any amount is withdrawable. Victim receives tokens but has no control over timing.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of control over withdrawal timing; potential tax/accounting implications for the victim.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `withdraw` to `msg.sender == user` or require a signature from `user`.

hypotheses.title: Bridge.processMessage reentrancy via _invokeMessageCall
hypotheses.description: `processMessage` calls `_invokeMessageCall` which performs an external call to `_message.to` with `_message.value`. The message status is updated to `DONE` or `RETRIABLE` after the call. If the called contract re-enters `processMessage` with the same `_message`, the `messageStatus[msgHash]` is still `NEW` (not yet updated), so the check `if (messageStatus[msgHash] != Status.NEW) revert B_STATUS_MISMATCH();` passes. The re-entrant call will then execute the message again, potentially draining funds or duplicating effects. The `nonReentrant` modifier on `processMessage` prevents this specific reentrancy, but the `_invokeMessageCall` is also called from `retryMessage` which is `nonReentrant`. However, the context is stored and reset around the call, and the `nonReentrant` guard is on the external function, so reentrancy into `processMessage` is blocked. The real issue is that `_invokeMessageCall` can call back into `Bridge` via `onMessageInvocation` on a vault, which then calls `sendMessage` — but `sendMessage` is `nonReentrant` and the guard is active. So the reentrancy is blocked. The finding is that the status update happens after the external call, which is a code smell but not exploitable due to `nonReentrant`.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not exploitable due to `nonReentrant`.
hypotheses.impact: None.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move `_updateMessageStatus` before the external call for defense in depth.
